opus-5.5.text:
I think benchmarks are useful, but they're a means, not the goal. When a field is young, a good benchmark gives everyone a shared target, and that alignment really does accelerate progress. Many of the advances we've seen came from people grinding on a clear, measurable objective.

The problem starts when the benchmark becomes the thing you optimize directly. Then you get Goodhart's law: the score goes up, but the capability you actually care about doesn't necessarily move with it. You can overfit to the distribution of the test, learn its format, sometimes even get contamination from the training data. On paper the model looks stronger, but when a real user brings a messy, open-ended task, the gap shows immediately.

So internally, I'd rather treat benchmarks as a kind of health check than as the North Star. If a model is truly getting smarter, if its reasoning, long-context understanding, and ability to use tools and finish multi-step tasks are improving, the benchmark numbers will usually follow naturally. But the reverse isn't true. Chasing the numbers doesn't guarantee intelligence.

What matters more to me is whether the model creates real value: can it take a task a person actually has and complete it end to end? That's harder to measure, and I think one of the most important things right now is building better evaluations that are closer to real use. Things like agentic tasks, long-horizon work, environments where the model has to explore and correct itself. In a sense, the definition of the evaluation shapes the direction of the whole field, so choosing what to measure is itself a research taste question.

So my view is: respect benchmarks, use them, but don't let them define you. The real benchmark is whether users keep coming back.

r001.rationale: It says optimizing directly for a benchmark can lead to overfitting to the test distribution or format.

r002.rationale: It states the score can rise without the capability of interest improving, and that chasing scores does not guarantee intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Benchmark scores are a means, not the end. I think of a score as a thermometer: it tells you something about the temperature of the model, but if you start optimizing the thermometer itself, you lose the signal very quickly. At that point you're just fitting the test distribution, and the number stops telling you anything about whether the model actually got smarter.

What we care about is the underlying capability. If you push a model's general intelligence up, benchmarks go up as a side effect, and that's the healthy direction of causality. The unhealthy direction is when a team sets a target on a specific leaderboard and then does whatever it takes to hit that number: tuning on similar data, picking prompts carefully, cherry-picking the evaluation setup. You can get a very impressive chart and a model that users feel is no better, or even worse, in real conversations.

So internally, we use benchmarks mostly for diagnosis. They help you find where the model is weak and whether a training change moved things in the right direction. But we try hard not to make them the objective in the loss-function sense. Once a metric becomes a target, it stops being a good metric. The real test is whether the model generalizes to problems nobody wrote a test for yet, whether it can go longer on a hard task, whether it reasons rather than recalls.

The other thing is that benchmarks saturate. A lot of the classic ones are already close to ceiling, so the gap between two frontier models on those is basically noise. The interesting signal is now in the long tail: long-horizon agentic tasks, truly novel math or coding problems, and ultimately whether people choose to use the model every day. That last one is the benchmark that's hardest to game, and in the end it's the one that matters.

r001.rationale: It warns that optimizing a specific leaderboard can lead to fitting the test distribution, tuning on similar data, and cherry-picking the evaluation.

r002.rationale: It says a team can achieve an impressive benchmark chart while users feel the model is no better or even worse.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmark scores are useful, but they’re a proxy for what we actually care about. The goal is to make a model more capable and more useful to people. A benchmark gives us a relatively clear way to measure progress, but it only captures a slice of that goal.

Once you optimize heavily for a particular benchmark, you have to ask whether the model is developing a general capability or just getting better at that particular test. Those can look similar in the score, but they have very different implications.

So I would look at benchmarks alongside performance on unfamiliar tasks and real user problems. If those improve together, that’s a strong signal. If the score goes up but users don’t experience an improvement, then we need to reconsider what we’re measuring.

r001.rationale: It warns that optimizing heavily for a particular benchmark may improve performance on that test without building general capability.

r002.rationale: It says a benchmark score can go up while users experience no improvement, showing that a higher score need not reflect genuine improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmark scores are useful signals, but they’re not the ultimate objective. A benchmark measures a particular set of tasks, and improving on those tasks doesn’t necessarily mean the model is more useful in practice. If you focus too narrowly on the score, you can end up optimizing for the test rather than the underlying capability.

What matters is whether the improvement generalizes. Can the model handle unfamiliar problems? Can it reliably complete the tasks users actually care about? Higher benchmark scores are valuable when they reflect progress on those things. So I would use benchmarks as feedback, alongside real-world evaluation, rather than treat the number itself as the goal.

r001.rationale: It warns that focusing too narrowly on benchmark scores can mean “optimizing for the test rather than the underlying capability,” identifying the risk of overfitting to the benchmark.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark gains do not necessarily mean the model is more useful or has improved in underlying capability, so scores can rise without genuine broader improvement.
